title: Iliff Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Iliff wells have a median depth of 80 feet; see local yields, water levels, drilling costs, permits, and risks before buying.
h1: Iliff, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Drilling Costs
intro_html:
Buying land near Iliff means evaluating the well, not just the house or acreage. Colorado DWR records within 5 miles show 555 permitted wells, with 375 recorded as constructed. Most are shallow by Colorado standards, but the local records also include deeper wells and a wide range of reported yields.

This page uses the available permit data for Iliff and nearby plains areas, including Padroni, Sterling, Fleming, and Peetz. Use the numbers to screen a property and compare a contractor's proposal, then verify the specific well permit, water right, pump system, and water quality before closing.

sections.heading: Iliff well depths are usually shallow, but the spread matters
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Iliff is 80 feet. The middle half runs from 52 to 130 feet, so a driller's bid for a typical location should not automatically be based on a deep mountain-style well. Sixty percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 33% fall from 100 to 300 feet.

There are exceptions. The 90th-percentile depth is 260 feet, and the deepest well on record reaches 500 feet. Seven percent are in the 300-to-600-foot range, with none recorded above 600 feet. Local ground conditions include alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, so the exact depth depends on the site, the target aquifer, casing and grout requirements, and what nearby well logs show.

sections.heading: Reported Iliff yields are strong, with limited testing coverage
sections.html:
Among the 102 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half spans 15.0 to 1375.0 gallons per minute, an unusually broad range that tells a buyer not to rely on the median alone. Ninety percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute, while 10% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute in this dataset. That is encouraging, but only a portion of the 555 permitted wells report a yield. Ask for the well completion report and a current pump test. Household demand, livestock, irrigation, storage, and pressure-system sizing are separate questions from the well's tested production.

sections.heading: Iliff water levels show a deeper recent measurement pattern
sections.html:
The median static water level is 20 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 12 and 45 feet. That is a useful starting point for pump setting, trench planning, and understanding how much lift the system may need, but it is not a guarantee for a new hole or an operating well.

The recorded measurements point to a deeper water level in the newer decade: the median was 26 feet below surface in the 2010s and 48 feet in the 2020s. That suggests water was measured farther down in the more recent records, but only 33 wells report a static water level. Treat it as a local warning to check current conditions, not proof of a basin-wide decline. Seasonal timing, measurement methods, and individual well locations can affect the comparison.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use around Iliff
sections.html:
Iliff has a long permit record, with permits issued in every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s. The busiest decade in the records was the 2000s, with 99 permits. The 1970s had 61, the 1960s 51, the 1990s 46, the 2010s 44, the 1980s 33, the 1950s 32, and the 2020s 17. The newest permit year is 2026.

The most common recorded uses are domestic or household at 43%, stock at 36%, and irrigation at 25%; monitoring makes up 5%. Those categories can overlap in the local record, so confirm the permitted use before assuming a well can serve a residence, livestock, lawn, or irrigation system. The most active named drillers are Stewart Drilling Co. (Stewart, Dennis W.), Canfield, Leslie George, and M&S Drilling, Inc. (Monheiser, Mark).

sections.heading: A typical Iliff well budget starts around the 80-foot median
sections.html:
For Iliff's alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, the drilling-rate model is $35 to $55 per foot. At the 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,800 to $4,400. That is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,800 to $16,400 at the median depth. A bid can move outside that range if the site needs a deeper hole, additional casing or grout, difficult access, longer utility runs, treatment equipment, or special surface completion. Have the contractor identify what is included, and compare the proposal with nearby well construction reports rather than using a countywide average.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic setbacks, and low-yield risk
sections.html:
Environmental screening matters before buying. Within about 10 miles, the mapped records include 8 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. There are 0 historic mine features. These mapped sites do not establish that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to order a laboratory water test and review the site's proximity and groundwater direction.

Low yield is not the only concern. A dry hole, poor construction, damaged casing, or inadequate grout can create a serious problem even where nearby wells are productive. Keep the well away from septic components as required by the design and local rules, and confirm that the lot has room for a permitted septic system, replacement area, driveway, utilities, and the home footprint. A Colorado DWR permit and any augmentation requirement also need review before construction.

sections.heading: Before buying an Iliff lot, verify the exact well record
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's DWR permit number and completion report. Confirm total depth, casing, pump, permitted use, reported yield, and the date and depth of any water-level measurement. Then compare several nearby records, especially in Padroni, Sterling, Fleming, or Peetz only as local context, not as substitutes for the subject property.

For an existing home, inspect the pressure tank, controls, electrical service, storage, and water quality. For raw land, get a driller's site-specific estimate and have septic feasibility checked before committing to a house plan. The 80-foot median supports a relatively modest initial drilling allowance, but the 260-foot 90th percentile shows why a contingency is necessary. If the proposed use extends beyond ordinary household needs, review the permit terms, water rights, and any augmentation-plan issue with the appropriate professional.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Iliff, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Iliff is 80 feet. The middle half is 52 to 130 feet, and 60% are under 100 feet. Some are much deeper: the 90th-percentile depth is 260 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 500 feet. The specific property and aquifer control the final depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Iliff?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $35 to $55 per foot in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At Iliff's 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,800 to $4,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $8,800 to $16,400. Deeper drilling, access, casing, and utility distance can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Iliff wells produce?
faq.a: Of the 102 local wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. Ninety percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 10% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 5 gallons per minute. Because many permits do not report yield, request a pump test for the specific well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Iliff?
faq.a: Permit records do not prove that water is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles of Iliff, the mapped environmental records include 8 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well through a laboratory before relying on it for drinking, and review the result with a qualified water professional if anything is elevated.

faq.q: Are Iliff water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The available records show a deeper median measured water level in the newer decade: 26 feet below surface in the 2010s compared with 48 feet in the 2020s. Only 33 wells report static water levels, so this is a limited signal rather than proof of a basin-wide decline. Check the subject well's measurement date, condition, and current pump performance before drawing conclusions.
